title: Efficacy of erector spinae plane block for patients with inflammatory bowel disease undergoing major abdominal surgery: A double-blind randomized controlled trial
content:
by Yasmin Alhamdah, Yehoshua Gleicher, Hermann dos Santos Fernandes, Sharon Peacock, Xiang Y. Ye, Christopher Brown, Anthony de Buck van Overstraeten, Zeev Friedman, Naveed Siddiqui

Objectives

Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) undergoing abdominal surgery face challenges in postoperative recovery due to high opioid needs and limited analgesic alternatives. The erector spinae plane (ESP) block has been shown to improve recovery in abdominal procedures, but its efficacy in the IBD population remains unknown. We investigated whether bilateral ESP blocks improve postoperative quality of recovery in this population.

Methods

In this prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, adults with IBD scheduled for elective laparoscopic-assisted abdominal surgery were randomized to receive bilateral ESP blocks with either 0.5% ropivacaine or normal saline before induction of anesthesia. The primary outcome was quality of recovery assessed using the 15-item QoR (QoR-15) scale at postoperative day (POD) 2. Secondary outcomes included QoR-15 at POD 1 and 3, pain scores (VAS), opioid consumption, opioid-related side effects, and hospital length of stay.

Results

Fifty-seven patients were randomized and analyzed: 31 in the ropivacaine group and 26 in the saline group. Baseline characteristics were generally similar between groups. The postoperative QoR-15, defined as the average QoR-15 scores over POD 1–3, was 10.2 points higher in the intervention group although not statistically significant (p = 0.27). The intervention group had a smaller decline in postoperative QoR-15 scores compared to controls (mean difference in the change of postoperative QoR-15 from baseline = 19.9 points; 95% CI: 2.3 to 37.5; p = 0.02). Baseline-adjusted longitudinal analysis also suggested higher QoR-15 scores on POD 2 in the intervention group (28.9-point difference; 95% CI: 3.9 to 53.8; p = 0.02). However, these adjusted findings should be interpreted cautiously because the confidence intervals were wide, indicating limited precision. Pain scores and opioid consumption were similar between groups. Constipation was less frequent in the intervention group on POD 2 (p = 0.041). No significant differences were found in hospital length of stay.

Conclusion

The unadjusted primary comparison of postoperative QoR-15 at POD2 was not statistically significant; however, the intervention group scored numerically higher by 23 points, a substantial difference in magnitude that was consistent with the statistically significant effects observed in both change score and longitudinal mixed-effects analyses. Bilateral ESP blocks did not significantly reduce postoperative pain or opioid use. Taken together, these findings suggest a possible, clinically meaningful recovery benefit that should be considered exploratory and requires confirmation in larger multicenter trials with early postoperative analgesic assessment and block-success verification.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT06230003.
